meta.name: Employee Creator
meta.title: From Zero to Production: A Solo Full-Stack HR System with Spring Boot and React
meta.description: A full-stack CRUD system for tracking employee records and immutable contract history, built solo in 4 weeks to prove production-grade full-stack practices.
meta.myRole: Solo full-stack developer -backend API, frontend, testing strategy, CI/CD, and AWS deployment

highlights.tagline: Solo full-stack HR system built and deployed to live AWS infrastructure in 4 weeks.
highlights.signatureQuote: Contracts are immutable by design -no update endpoint- so a legal record can't be silently edited, only appended to.

problem: HR teams managing employee records need a system that separates day-to-day employee updates from an immutable, auditable contract history. Most CRUD tutorials handle a single entity type, not the compliance-relevant split between mutable employee info and legal contract documents that must never be silently edited after creation.

architectureDecisions.decision: Modeled employees and contracts as a one-to-many relationship, with contracts treated as immutable (no update endpoint).
architectureDecisions.why: Employee details (salary, department, hours) change routinely, but a contract is a legal document that shouldn't be silently edited after the fact -separating the tables keeps casual updates from touching auditable history.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: Any change to contract terms has to be a new contract row rather than a field update, pushing more display logic onto the frontend to render contract history correctly.

architectureDecisions.decision: Used a hybrid testing approach: top-down TDD on the backend, but manual browser testing before writing frontend tests.
architectureDecisions.why: Full top-down TDD on both layers was too slow for a solo 4-week timeline. The backend's business rules (contract immutability, employee/contract relationships) benefited most from tests-first; the UI benefited more from fast manual iteration.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: Frontend test coverage is thinner and arrived later than the backend's -visible in the 'React tests still in progress' known issue.

architectureDecisions.decision: Migrated the live demo deployment from AWS (EC2 + S3/CloudFront) to Render, with the demo database swapped from MySQL to Render's free-tier Postgres.
architectureDecisions.why: The AWS free tier backing the original demo deployment expired; Render offers a more generous, ongoing free tier for a small demo workload without having to keep managing EC2 directly.
architectureDecisions.tradeoff: The live demo now runs on Postgres rather than the MySQL the app was actually designed, seeded, and tested against, and this is a demo-only substitution -the architecture described above and in the backend README still reflects the original AWS/MySQL design, not what the current live link is running on.

hardestProblem.issue: Once the backend and frontend were deployed to separate AWS services (EC2 for the API, S3 + CloudFront for the React app), the frontend couldn't reach the API -requests were failing between the two origins.
hardestProblem.diagnosis: Traced it to two separate causes stacked on top of each other: an overly restrictive CORS configuration on the Spring Boot side, and the EC2 instance's security group not allowing the right inbound traffic on the API's port.
hardestProblem.fix: Explicitly allowlisted the deployed frontend's exact origin in the Spring CORS config instead of a wildcard, adjusted the EC2 security group rules, and put Nginx in front of the app as a reverse proxy with TLS via Certbot so the API is only reachable through the expected domain and port.
hardestProblem.result: The two separately-hosted services now communicate reliably over HTTPS, and the CORS/security-group fix is documented in the backend README so it doesn't have to be rediscovered on a future redeploy.

metrics.label: Automated tests
metrics.value: 40+ tests -JUnit/Mockito unit tests plus REST Assured/H2 integration tests covering employees and contracts

metrics.label: CI/CD
metrics.value: Two GitHub Actions pipelines (Spring Boot test suite, React deploy) running on push

metrics.label: Production footprint
metrics.value: Backend on EC2 with JVM heap capped at 256MB and a trimmed MySQL buffer pool so Nginx, the JVM, and MySQL fit on one small instance; frontend on S3 + CloudFront

outcome.limitations: Contract deletion isn't fully wired up in the frontend yet, employee list pagination is still missing so larger lists mean bigger API payloads, the employee list doesn't auto-refresh after a delete without a manual reload, and React component test coverage is still described as basic -all tracked as known issues rather than glossed over.

whatIdDoDifferently: Add pagination to the employee list earlier -it's a known issue now, but it should have been part of the initial API design before contract history started growing response sizes.

Move the contract form's employee-ID field out of manual free-text entry sooner; leaving it as a raw input is a documented UX risk for human error that a dropdown or auto-fill would have avoided from the start.

Write React component tests alongside each feature instead of after -the browser-test-first approach was the right call for solo speed, but backfilling Vitest tests later is why frontend coverage lagged the backend's.
Unify the two deploy pipelines -the frontend redeploys automatically through GitHub Actions while the backend redeploy is a manual package-and-restart, which is an avoidable inconsistency.
